content.title: About
content.content: Bacon is cured, smoked pork meat, usually taken from the belly or back. It has a distinctive aroma, rich flavor, and becomes crispy when fried. Bacon is commonly used as a topping for sandwiches, salads, soups, and many other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon has been part of cuisine since ancient Rome, where pork was salted and air‑dried.
The word “bacon” comes from the Old French “bacon,” meaning “pork, bacon.”
In the United States more than 18 million tons of bacon are consumed each year.
Bacon is a popular ingredient in culinary experiments, including desserts and cocktails.
Smoking bacon can be done hot or cold, which influences its flavor and texture.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Bacon provides high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc helps maintain immune function and participates in protein metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Presence of fatty acids
items.content: Bacon includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Bacon is salty, which can raise blood pressure if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A large amount of saturated fat may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: Smoking often involves nitrites, which can be harmful in high doses.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bacon is calorie‑dense, so portion control is important, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bacon is usually fried until crisp and added to sandwiches, salads, omelets, or used as a flavoring ingredient in soups and vegetable dishes. It can also be baked in the oven or cooked in a microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bacon in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for up to 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 6 months. Before use, check the smell and color: discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

beef-dumplings-and-vegetables-excluding-.title: Beef, dumplings, and vegetables (no carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy) with gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender beef, boiled dumplings and a selection of vegetables, excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens. All components are served with a savory gravy made from beef broth.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of iron and vitamin B12.
Traditional Russian dumplings are often made with a mix of beef and pork, but this version uses only beef.
Leaving out carrots, broccoli and leafy greens highlights milder vegetables such as sweet pepper, zucchini or cauliflower.
Gravy prepared from beef stock enhances the meat flavor and keeps the dish juicy.
The meal is commonly served in colder seasons as a hearty lunch or dinner.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and dumplings provide high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is rich in vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish fits moderate low‑carb diets as the main carbohydrate source is the dumplings.

items.title: Beneficial vegetables
items.content: Vegetables like sweet pepper and zucchini add fiber, vitamin C and antioxidants.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Beef and meat dumplings can contain saturated fats; people with cardiovascular concerns should watch portion size.

items.title: Salt in gravy
items.content: Gravy is often seasoned with salt; those with hypertension should limit added salt.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Dumpling dough typically contains wheat, which may be problematic for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: Large pieces of beef can be hard to digest for people with gastrointestinal issues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot. Boil the dumplings until they float, slice the beef thinly, and lightly sauté or steam the vegetables. Pour the gravy over everything and optionally garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Dumplings and beef can be frozen separately for up to 3 months. Keep the gravy in a separate container and reheat before serving.

chicken-or-turkey-and-rice-with-soy-base.title: Chicken or Turkey with Rice and Soy‑Based Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of boiled or baked chicken or turkey meat served with steamed rice and a soy‑based sauce made from fermented soybeans. The sauce gives a savory, slightly sweet umami flavor, while the rice provides a light, fluffy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are complete protein sources, containing all essential amino acids.
Soy sauce originated in China over 2,500 years ago as a method of preserving food.
Rice is the primary carbohydrate staple in Asian cuisine; varieties include white, brown, basmati, and jasmine.
The combination of meat, rice, and soy sauce is a hallmark of stir‑fry dishes popular worldwide.
When cooked properly, rice retains a good amount of B‑vitamins, and soy sauce adds small amounts of iron and magnesium.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (when using breast meat)
items.content: Skin‑less poultry contains little saturated fat, making the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the meat and rice supply niacin (B3), B6, and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: Meat and soy sauce contribute these minerals, important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index of rice
items.content: When paired with protein and sauce, rice promotes satiety and a steadier blood‑sugar response.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional soy sauce is salty; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Proper cooking of poultry
items.content: Chicken and turkey should reach an internal temperature of 75 °C to prevent salmonella.

items.title: Rice quality control
items.content: Some rice batches may contain trace heavy metals; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, optionally topped with fresh vegetables (broccoli, carrots, green onions) or a sprinkle of sesame seeds. Adjust sauce amount to taste. For a lighter version, use brown rice and low‑sodium soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the microwave or skillet with a splash of water to prevent drying out. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months.

chicken-thigh-baked-or-broiled-skin-not-.title: Chicken thigh, baked or broiled, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh is the meat from the upper leg of a chicken, prepared by baking or broiling without the skin. In fast‑food restaurants and casual dining it is often served as a portioned main, a topping for salads, or in sandwiches. Thigh meat is juicier and more flavorful than breast meat because of its higher natural fat content, yet removing the skin keeps the calorie count moderate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thigh contains more iron and zinc than chicken breast.
When baked without skin, some of the fat melts away, making it less fatty than fried skin‑on thighs.
In the United States, skinless thighs are a common component of BBQ and fried‑chicken dishes.
Skinless thigh meat is considered a better option for lower‑fat diets while retaining a rich taste.
In Japan, skinless chicken thighs are sometimes used for tempura, giving a light, crispy coating.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Skinless thigh provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function, metabolism, and wound healing.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb and keto diets when sauces are controlled.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports thyroid function.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Restaurant preparations often add salt and sauces, raising sodium levels, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Higher saturated fat when fried
items.content: If thighs are deep‑fried, saturated fat content increases, which may be undesirable for heart‑health diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh can be served hot as a main dish, sliced for salads, added to sandwiches, or tossed into soups. When baked, season with herbs, spices, and a drizzle of olive oil. In restaurants it is often accompanied by yogurt‑based, mustard, or tomato sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh thighs should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen thighs store well for up to 9 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge, not at room temperature. Cooked leftovers belong in an airtight container and should be eaten within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked duck egg is a fully boiled egg obtained from a duck. The egg is larger and has a brighter orange yolk compared with a chicken egg. It offers a richer, slightly sweet flavor and a firmer white texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Duck eggs are typically 1.5–2 times larger than chicken eggs.
The yolk contains more vitamin A and fat‑soluble vitamins than chicken yolk.
In many Asian cuisines duck eggs are considered a delicacy and are used in dishes such as Chinese "pao jing".
Uncooked duck eggs can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 4 weeks.
In 1949 duck eggs gained popularity in post‑war Europe as a protein source.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: One cooked duck egg provides about 13 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: The yolk is a good source of retinol, important for vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Duck eggs contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: They provide iron, phosphorus and selenium, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Cooked duck egg supplies vitamin D and calcium, contributing to bone strength.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People allergic to egg proteins may react to duck eggs as well.

items.title: High cholesterol
items.content: One egg contains roughly 370 mg of cholesterol, so individuals with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Risk of salmonella
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial contamination even after cooking.

items.title: Higher calorie count
items.content: A duck egg is more caloric (about 180 kcal) than a chicken egg, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked duck egg can be eaten plain, sliced into salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a filling for sushi. It is often served with soy sauce, vinegar, or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep boiled duck eggs in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Discard any that develop an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat with tomato-based sauce is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of cooked or stewed meat covered with a thick sauce made from tomatoes, spices, and sometimes vegetables. It is convenient for quick meal preparation while preserving the flavor and nutritional value of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives it the characteristic red color.
Traditionally, meat in tomato sauce was prepared in Mediterranean cuisine, where the meat‑tomato combination is classic.
The taste and texture vary depending on the type of meat (beef, pork, chicken).
Herbs such as basil, oregano, and thyme are often added to enhance the aroma.
The product can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or frozen for up to 3 months.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties and supports heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the meat and tomato sauce supply B6, B12, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The product fits low‑carb diets as most calories come from protein and fat.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or spices.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Poor‑quality or improperly processed meat can be a source of pathogens.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Ready‑made products may contain additives and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in the microwave or on the stove and serve with a side such as rice, potatoes, pasta, or vegetables. It also works well in casseroles, soups, and sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in a sealed container for no more than 5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before use, check for any off‑odors indicating spoilage.

rice-brown-with-cheese-and-or-cream-base.title: Brown Rice with Cheese and/or Cream Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains the bran and germ layers. In this version it is served with a cheese and/or cream sauce to which fat (oil or butter) has been added, increasing its energy density and giving a richer mouthfeel.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains more nutrients than white rice, including fiber, B‑vitamins and minerals.
Cheese sauces are often made from processed cheese, cream and spices, creating a smooth, creamy texture.
Adding fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as D and K.
In some Asian cuisines brown rice is combined with dairy products, creating unique hybrid dishes.
When stored properly, brown rice can stay fresh for up to 6 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood glucose levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy, beneficial for active individuals and athletes.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fat enhances vitamin absorption
items.content: The added fat aids the body’s uptake of fat‑soluble vitamins present in cheese and cream.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Brown rice supplies magnesium, phosphorus and iron, important for muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat and cheese sauce significantly increase the dish’s calories, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese and cream sauces may contain lactose, making the dish unsuitable for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to cheese or cream.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared cheese sauces often contain salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish with meat, fish or vegetable stews, use as a base for casseroles, or toss into salads. It pairs well with herbs, spices (black pepper, paprika) and a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

rice-brown-with-corn-no-added-fat.title: Brown Rice with Corn, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice mixed with whole corn kernels is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ of the rice while adding crunchy corn pieces. It contains no added fat, making it a low‑calorie option suitable for many dietary plans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice preserves more nutrients than white rice because the bran and germ are intact.
Corn adds a subtle sweetness and a pleasant crunch to the blend.
The mix is popular in Asian and Latin American cuisines as a side dish or salad base.
The absence of added fat makes it a good choice for calorie‑conscious eaters.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while selenium offers antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Brown rice raises blood sugar more slowly than white rice, beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Corn antioxidants
items.content: Corn is rich in carotenoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Like any grain, rice may contain trace heavy metals; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the rice in a 1:2.5 water ratio until tender, use it in salads, pilafs, or as a base for vegetable stir‑fries. Enhance flavor with herbs, spices, or a splash of soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to prevent mold growth.
